lines.text: Atlanta hums with nervous energy as Belgium walk out for what could be the final act of their golden generation's World Cup story. Against them stand the All Whites of New Zealand.
But before the first whistle, a question rings out over the city. Long before this team, an old nation had a sound for its triumphs and its farewells. Hold on to that sound.
Welcome back to WorldCup twenty-six Legends — episode sixty-eight. Belgium, versus New Zealand. Group G. The last stand.
A decade of brilliance against a nation of five million. De Bruyne knows the maths: win and they advance. Anything less, and a golden era ends in silence.
Belgium — the Red Devils. Red, the last great act of a generation told for ten years they were destined for greatness, and still chasing the trophy to prove it.
Kevin De Bruyne, thirty-four, the maestro, still threading passes no one else can see. Romelu Lukaku, the tank, his country's record scorer with the hunger of a man written off too many times.
Jérémy Doku, the spark on the wing. Youri Tielemans, the engine. And behind them Thibaut Courtois, six foot six, standing in goal like a lighthouse over a dark sea.
New Zealand — the All Whites. White, a nation of five million who refuse to believe they don't belong, carried by a captain who completed a plumbing apprenticeship before football called.
Chris Wood does not care about Belgium's legacy. A target man of the old school — aerial, clinical — he carries his country with the quiet certainty of a man with nothing to lose.
So here it is. A golden generation's coronation, or a street fight it might not survive. The maestro's vision against the plumber's header.
And one duel defines the night — De Bruyne's mind against Wood, the giant who needs only one cross, one leap, one moment.
And before the moment that rattles the crossbar — stay with me. Because first, the Red Devils show their class.
Here is how we see it. Belgium strike first — and then a nation of five million refuses to go quietly.
Around twenty-five minutes, Lukaku bullies his way through and smashes it home. Belgium, one — New Zealand, nil. The golden generation, exactly to plan.
But on fifty-five minutes, a cross swings in and Chris Wood climbs highest, the header thumping into the net. One — one. Five million dare to dream the impossible.
Belgium answer like champions. De Bruyne steps up on seventy minutes and curls one into the corner — that left foot, still magic. Two — one, Red Devils. But it is not over.
Eighty-fifth minute. New Zealand throw everyone forward. A long ball drops, Wood climbs above two defenders. Courtois leaps, a fingertip — and the ball crashes off the crossbar.
The bar trembles. The rebound falls, one shot, one moment — and the thread holds. Belgium survive, two to one, by the width of a crossbar.
A decade of brilliance, reduced to a rebound in the eighty-fifth minute. The golden generation's last stand was never going to be a coronation — only a survival.
That is our prediction — Belgium, two to one. The thread held, by a crossbar. Not played yet — the real ninety minutes are yours to watch.
Because that is the beautiful cruelty of the World Cup: it lets you choose your ending, but only by surviving the one your opponent is fighting to give you.
A generation of giants, a nation of five million, and a bar still trembling. Tonight the thread holds. Tomorrow, the World Cup makes no promises.
Do you agree? Comment DIABLES if the golden generation survives. Comment ALL WHITES if a plumber's header deserved to break Belgian hearts.

That sound. The towns of Belgium had the carillon — bronze bells that have rung for every triumph and farewell for five hundred years. Tonight they ring for a generation's last stand. Legend sixty-eight. The Carillonneur. The sound of an old nation.
The players carry the legacy. The Carillonneur carries the sound of it. And this Legend is not just to watch — it is yours to claim, and to collect.

Then pick three of the forty-eight nations, and every goal they score, scores for you. Free to play, just for fun. No prizes — only glory.
